findings.claim: “Part 1 asks you to analyse an extract closely (AO1 + AO2).” Part 2 is described with no assessment objective at all.
findings.truth: On the 19th-century novel question, part (a) carries 20 marks for AO2 alone and part (b) carries 20 marks for AO1 alone. Naming AO1 on the extract question sends students to write personal-response material that earns nothing there.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md: 'Assessment Objectives covered are AO1 and AO2' (Component 2 Section A) and the raw mark distribution table, Questions 1a to 7a = AO2 20, Questions 1b to 7b = AO1 20.

findings.claim: Practice question 2 ends “You must refer to the context of the novel in your answer.”
findings.truth: AO3 is not assessed anywhere in the 19th-century novel section, so the instruction directs students at an objective that carries no marks. It is an AQA rubric imported into an Edexcel unit.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md, Component 2 Section A: 'Assessment Objectives covered are AO1 and AO2'; AO3 appears only in Section B and in Component 1.

findings.claim: Magwitch's line “What was my character? Could I be a deserving poor?”, used 17 times across lessons 1, 4, 6 and 8 — in body text, a key fact, four mark schemes, three knowledge-check items and three flashcards.
findings.truth: The line does not exist in the novel. Neither 'deserving poor' nor 'was my character' appears in Magwitch's mouth anywhere in the text. The real passage that makes the same argument is his chapter 42 self-account: “But what the Devil was I to do? I must put something into my stomach, mustn't I?”
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1400: grep for 'deserving poor' returns nothing; ch. 42 line 14557-14559: 'They always went on agen me about the Devil. But what the Devil was I to do? I must put something into my stomach, mustn't I?'

findings.claim: “Suffering has been stronger than all other teaching” is given to Pip in lesson 1 (“Pip eventually learns”), lesson 5 (“Pip's line”), lesson 8 (“His own line”) and on three flashcards.
findings.truth: The line is Estella's, spoken to Pip in the closing chapter. Lesson 8's quotation bank already attributes it correctly to Estella, so the unit contradicts itself.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1400 ch. 59, lines 20409-20413: '“But you said to me,” returned Estella ... “now, when suffering has been stronger than all other teaching, and has taught me to understand what your heart used to be.”'

findings.claim: “The fire that consumes Miss Havisham ... becomes the instrument of her death”; “The wedding dress ... literally burns her alive”; and knowledge check 4 asks students to complete “Miss Havisham dies when her _____ catches fire”.
findings.truth: Pip smothers the flames with his coats and the table cloth and she survives. The surgeon judges the burns 'far from hopeless'; she is laid on the great table, speaks that evening, and dies much later — Joe reports her death to Pip in chapter 57.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1400 ch. 49, lines 16924-16955 (rescue and 'serious hurts, but ... far from hopeless'); ch. 53 line 17679 'she was still very ill, though considered something better'; ch. 57 lines 19551-19562 (Joe: 'she ain't living').

findings.claim: “Satis House is destroyed twice: first by Miss Havisham's fire, then by being demolished and sold.”
findings.truth: The fire burned Miss Havisham, not the building; she is treated in the same room minutes later. The house is sold as old building materials and pulled down after her death.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1400 ch. 49 line 16955 (bed carried into that room); ch. 59 line 19930 'be sold as old building materials, and pulled down. LOT 1'.

findings.claim: Pip is sent to Satis House “by his uncle Pumblechook”.
findings.truth: Pumblechook is Joe's uncle. Dickens flags this the first time he names him, and the point matters because Pip's household treats Pumblechook as a relative he has no blood tie to.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1400 ch. 4, lines 993-994: 'Uncle Pumblechook (Joe's uncle, but Mrs. Joe appropriated him)'.

findings.claim: Compeyson “jilted Miss Havisham at the altar” (lesson 4 body text and flashcard; lesson 6 glossary and its in-text definition).
findings.truth: Compeyson never came to the church. He sent a letter, which reached her at twenty minutes to nine while she was dressing — which is why the clocks stop at that time, a detail the unit itself relies on elsewhere.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1400 ch. 22 (Herbert's account) and ch. 8 lines 2424-2425: 'at twenty minutes to nine, and that a clock in the room had stopped at twenty minutes to nine'.

findings.claim: In London Pip is disturbed “by the hangman's noose on display” (repeated in a mark scheme).
findings.truth: There is no noose on display. A court officer offers to show Pip where the gallows was kept, where people were publicly whipped, and the Debtors' Door out of which the condemned came to be hanged.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1400 ch. 20, lines 6916-6917; the only 'noose' in the novel is the one Orlick throws over Pip's head in ch. 53.

findings.claim: For the Part 2 essay, “analysing the metaphor of being shaped by suffering shows strong AO2 skills”.
findings.truth: Part (b) carries AO1 only. Method analysis earns nothing there; what is rewarded is a critical response supported by precise textual reference.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md raw mark distribution: Component 2 Questions 1b to 7b, AO1 20, total 20.

findings.claim: “thirty-two prisoners are sentenced to death alongside Magwitch”.
findings.truth: Thirty-two is the total, Magwitch included, not thirty-two plus him.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1400 ch. 56, lines 19209-19210: 'two-and-thirty men and women put before the Judge to receive that sentence together. Foremost among the two-and-thirty was he'.

findings.claim: Knowledge check 2 asks which assessment objectives are tested in Part 1 and marks “AO1 and AO2” correct.
findings.truth: Part (a) is AO2 only, all 20 marks. The check taught a false exam fact and no option offered the right answer, so the question and its options both needed rebuilding. The correct index stays 1.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md raw mark distribution: Component 2 Questions 1a to 7a, AO2 20, total 20.

findings.claim: Mark schemes make contextual knowledge a band criterion — e.g. “Secure grasp of the Victorian class system as context for Pip's shame” in a top band, and “Thoughtful analysis with clear contextual understanding” as an upper band. Ten schemes across the unit reward context in some form.
findings.truth: AO3 is not assessed on this section, so no context can be credited. Context may still inform an AO1 or AO2 point, which is why the softer 'links to Victorian attitudes' phrasing is defensible. Two schemes that made context an explicit band requirement are corrected here. Options for the remaining eight: strip every context clause board-wide, or leave them as content suggestions. Recommendation: a single Edexcel-wide sweep of Section A mark schemes rather than unit-by-unit edits, so the wording stays consistent across the seven novel arms.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md, Component 2 Section A: 'Assessment Objectives covered are AO1 and AO2'.

findings.claim: Dramatic irony is defined as “the audience or reader is led to expect one outcome, only for the actual outcome to be dramatically different”, in the in-text definition and the glossary.
findings.truth: That describes a plot twist. Dramatic irony is the reader knowing something a character does not. A student who wrote the lesson's definition in an exam would misuse a core AO2 term.
findings.evidence: Standard literary definition; the lesson itself says Dickens 'encourages the reader to share this assumption', which rules out dramatic irony at that point in the novel.

findings.claim: All 48 practice questions in the unit carry the label “20 marks — Extract Analysis”, including 24 that give no extract and ask for a whole-novel essay (“Explore how Dickens presents ... in Great Expectations”).
findings.truth: The 19th-century novel question has two parts: an extract question and a whole-text essay. Labelling the essays 'Extract Analysis' hides the second task from students. The 24 whole-text items are relabelled '20 marks — Whole Text Essay'; the mark of 20 is right in both cases.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/english-literature-1ET0.md: 'a two part question, with the first part focussed on an extract of approximately 400 words. The second part is an essay question exploring the whole text.'

findings.claim: Every one of the 48 mark schemes runs the ladder 'Top band (17-20) / Upper band (13-16) / Top band (9-12) / Upper-mid band (5-8) / Lower-mid band (3-4) / Lower band (1-2)', so 'Top band' names both the 17-20 and the 9-12 tier.
findings.truth: The house ladder is Top / Upper-mid / Mid / Lower-mid / Low / Basic. Not edited here because the retro programme already carries a fleet-wide band-ladder relabel job, and 48 competing edits on the same strings would collide with it. Flagging so this unit is picked up by that sweep.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT.md house ladder; the duplicate label appears in all 48 schemes.

findings.claim: Pip's fortune is “built with money earned through hard labour in the penal colonies”.
findings.truth: Magwitch made the money after his sentence, as a sheep farmer and stock breeder in New South Wales, not as convict labour. The lesson's wider point stands, so this is recorded rather than edited.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1400 ch. 39: Magwitch's account of sheep-farming and stock-breeding in the new world.

summary: Eight lessons checked against the Edexcel 1ET0 spec and the Gutenberg text. Two fabrications run through the whole unit: an invented Magwitch quotation used 17 times, and Estella's closing line 'Suffering has been stronger than all other teaching' repeatedly given to Pip. Exam framing is AQA-shaped throughout: AO1 credited on the AO2-only extract question, AO2 credited on the AO1-only whole-text essay, an 'you must refer to the context' rubric on a section where AO3 is not assessed, and every whole-text essay labelled 'Extract Analysis'. Plot errors: Miss Havisham killed off in the fire she actually survives, Satis House burned down, Compeyson jilting her at the altar, and Pumblechook made Pip's uncle.
